title: Physical Properties of Matter and Density
seo_title: Secondary 1 Science: Physical Properties and Density Worksheets with Answers
standard_code: Secondary 1: Exploring Diversity of Matter by its Physical Properties
standard_text: Describe physical properties such as electrical and thermal conductivity, melting and boiling point, strength, hardness, flexibility and density; classify objects and choose materials using property data; measure length, mass and volume, use displacement for irregular objects, calculate density (mass/volume) and predict whether an object sinks or floats (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 1 science worksheets for Singapore students on physical properties of matter: conductivity, melting point, hardness, density calculations, displacement and floating. With answers.
key_sub: Less dense than the liquid: it floats. Denser: it sinks.
body_html:
How to think about it

Physical properties can be observed or measured without changing what the substance is.

  • Examples: electrical and thermal conductivity, melting and boiling point, strength, hardness, flexibility and density.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume, in g/cm³ or kg/m³. It depends on the material, not the size.
  • An object floats in a liquid that is denser than it, and sinks in one that is less dense.
  • Volume of an irregular object = rise in water level in a measuring cylinder (displacement).
Example

Mass 54 g, volume 20 cm³. Density?

54 ÷ 20

Answer: 2.7 g/cm³

Example

Water rises from 40 cm³ to 52 cm³ when a stone is added. Volume of the stone?

52 − 40

Answer: 12 cm³

Common mistakes

  • Dividing volume by mass. Density = mass ÷ volume.
  • Thinking heavy objects always sink. A big log floats; a small coin sinks.
  • Taking the final reading as the volume of the object. Subtract the first reading.
  • Thinking that a hard material is always strong. Glass is hard but brittle.

faq.a: Divide the mass by the volume. The unit is g/cm³ or kg/m³.

faq.q: How do you find the volume of an irregular object?
faq.a: Put it into water in a measuring cylinder. The rise in the water level is its volume.

faq.q: Why does ice float on water?
faq.a: Ice (0.92 g/cm³) is less dense than water (1.0 g/cm³).
